Molten.name: Molten
Molten.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries, rounded: the chart has 4,567 (the oldest grains in meteorites, ratified 2022) and 4,031 ± 3 (the oldest rock, Acasta, since 2023)
Molten.officialName: Hadean, after Hades, the Greek god of the dead and the underworld he ruled; named by Preston Cloud in 1972
Molten.knownFrom: a few zircon crystals, smaller than grains of sand, and some moon rocks and meteorites
Molten.insideIt: events *Oldest grains*, *Gathering*, *Moon formed*, *Black Earth*, *Blue Earth*, *Grey Earth* (at the end edge). Plots: *Day length* and the inside line of *Sun and inside* begin at *Moon formed*; *Minerals*, *Continents* and the Sun line begin at 4,567.
Molten.picturesWanted: a painting of the magma ocean with the close Moon (NASA or ESA artwork; licence to check); a Jack Hills zircon in cathodoluminescence (John Valley, University of Wisconsin; licence to ask).
Molten.summary: The whole surface of the Earth was melted rock, under a sky of steam. Within a few million years it froze over, the steam rained down, and there was a sea. The Moon was new.

more.spanLine: From about 4.6 to 4 billion years ago.
paragraphs: At the start of this stretch there was nowhere to stand. The whole surface of the Earth was melted rock, glowing, and perhaps hundreds of kilometres deep. Above it hung air made of rock vapour and steam. The Earth had just been hit by another young planet, and the Moon had formed from the wreck (*Moon formed*). Through a gap in the steam, the Moon might have looked fifteen or twenty times wider than it does now, because it was that much closer.

The name *Molten* fits only the beginning. Models say the surface froze over within a few million years. Then the steam rained out, and the Earth had a sea. At first the sea was far hotter than boiling water. It stayed liquid because the thick air above it pressed down so hard.

By 4.4 billion years ago there was probably cool water at the surface. A crystal that formed then still remembers it (*Blue Earth*). So for nearly all of these 600 million years the Earth had a solid crust and a sea, and rocks from space kept falling on both.
What is new in this stretch is the planet itself: the Earth, with its Moon, then a crust, then a sea.

Almost nothing from it survives. There is no rock from most of it, only tiny crystals of zircon, a mineral so hard that it outlasts the rock it grew in. The oldest rock that nearly every geologist accepts formed beside the Acasta River in northern Canada, about 4.03 billion years ago (*Grey Earth*). That rock marks the end of this stretch.
Six hundred million years is about an eighth of the Earth's whole life. It is five sixths as long as the whole Animals line, from the first animals to now.
Geologists call this stretch the Hadean ("hay-DEE-un"), after Hades, the Greek god of the dead and the underworld he ruled. Preston Cloud, an American geologist, gave it the name in 1972.
Whether anything was alive in it, nobody knows.

references: Kevin Zahnle and others, "Emergence of a habitable planet," *Space Science Reviews*, 2007. The magma ocean freezing, the steam raining out, the hot sea under heavy air, the close Moon.

Simon Wilde, John Valley, William Peck and Colin Graham, "Evidence from detrital zircons for the existence of continental crust and oceans on the Earth 4.4 Gyr ago," *Nature*, 2001. Water by 4.4 billion.
Jaana Halla and others, "Ratification of the base of the ICS Geological Time Scale: the GSSA for the Hadean lower boundary," *Episodes*, 2024. The official start.
Robert Hazen, *The Story of Earth* (Viking, 2012). For a parent.

Oceans.name: Oceans
Oceans.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries: 4,000 is our rounding of the chart's 4,031 ± 3; 2,500 is a boundary fixed by agreement (1990), not by a layer of rock
Oceans.officialName: Archean, from the Greek for "ancient", which comes from the word for "beginning"; named by James Dwight Dana in 1872
Oceans.knownFrom: the oldest surviving rock, from about 4 billion years ago, and mounds built by microbes, from about 3.4 billion
Oceans.insideIt: events *Grey Earth* (at the start edge), *Bombardment*, *Stromatolites*, *Kenorland*, *Cyanobacteria* (at the end edge). Plots: *Oxygen* (begins at 4,000, near nothing), *Continents* (land a few hundredths of the surface), *Sun and inside*, *Day length*, *Minerals*.
Oceans.picturesWanted: the stromatolites at Strelley Pool, Pilbara (Geological Survey of Western Australia or Commons; licence to check); living stromatolites at Hamelin Pool, Shark Bay, as a picture of what the mounds were like (Commons; licence to check).
Oceans.summary: A world of sea, with a few low islands and almost no other dry land. There was no oxygen in the air. In shallow water, microbes built mounds, some of the oldest life we can point to.

more.spanLine: From about 4 to 2.5 billion years ago.
paragraphs: In the Pilbara of Western Australia, near a waterhole called Strelley Pool, there is rock that was once the floor of a shallow sea. In it are low mounds and cones, row on row for kilometres. Microbes probably built them, about 3.4 billion years ago, layer on layer, as living mats caught grains of sand and grew up through them (*Stromatolites*).

Stand on that sea floor and almost everything around is water. For most of this stretch there was very little dry land, mostly small islands. By some estimates, even near its end only two or three parts in a hundred of the Earth's surface stood above the sea. Today it is about thirty.
The air held no oxygen to breathe. Nobody knows the colour of the sky. Near the end, a haze may have come and gone, each time for less than a million years.

The Sun was about a fifth dimmer than now, yet the sea did not freeze. Why not is still argued. The days were short. Layers laid down by the tides in South Africa, about 3.2 billion years ago, have been read as days of thirteen to fifteen hours, though the geologists who read them disagree.

What is new in this stretch is rock that survives, and life we can point to. Before it there are only crystals; from it there are whole mountainsides. And in its rocks are the oldest signs of life that most geologists accept.

All of that life was microbes, each too small to see. Near the end, some of them were probably already using sunlight to split water and give off oxygen, but almost none of the oxygen reached the air (*Cyanobacteria*).
A billion and a half years is a third of the Earth's whole life. It is about twice as long as the Animals line.

Geologists call this stretch the Archean ("ar-KEE-un"), from the Greek word for "ancient", which comes from the word for "beginning". James Dwight Dana, an American geologist, gave it the name in 1872.

Nicolas Flament, Nicolas Coltice and Patrice Rey, "A case for late-Archaean continental emergence from thermal evolution models and hypsometry," *Earth and Planetary Science Letters*, 2008. How little land there was.
Aubrey Zerkle and others, "A bistable organic-rich atmosphere on the Neoarchaean Earth," *Nature Geoscience*, 2012. The haze that came and went.
Andrew Knoll, *A Brief History of Earth* (Custom House, 2021). For a parent.

Oxygen.name: Oxygen
Oxygen.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries fixed by agreement (1990), not by layers of rock
Oxygen.officialName: the first part of the Proterozoic, "earlier life" (from Greek *proteros*, earlier, and *zoe*, life), named by Samuel Franklin Emmons in the late 1880s; geologists split this part into the Siderian, Rhyacian and Orosirian, from Greek words for iron, a stream of lava and a range of mountains
Oxygen.knownFrom: rock that records the air: red soils and sandstones, banded iron, and sulphur in shale
Oxygen.insideIt: events *Cyanobacteria* (at the start edge), *Short days*, *Great freeze*, *Oxygen in the air*, *Red rocks*, *Banded iron*, *Nuna* (at the end edge). Plots: *Oxygen* (the rise at about 2,430 and the coming and going to about 2,220), *Day length* (about 17 hours at 2,460), *Minerals*.
Oxygen.picturesWanted: the banded iron walls of Joffre Gorge or Dales Gorge, Karijini (Commons or Parks and Wildlife WA; licence to check); a polished slab of banded iron (Commons; licence to check).
Oxygen.summary: Stripes of iron were settling on the sea floor, and ice came and went. Then, for the first time, oxygen stayed in the air. There was only a little, but it turned the ground red.

more.spanLine: From about 2.5 to 1.8 billion years ago.
paragraphs: In Karijini, in the Pilbara of Western Australia, the walls of Joffre Gorge are striped. Reddish-brown bands rich in iron lie between grey and white ones, thousands of them, each laid down on the floor of a sea about 2.46 billion years ago. They record slow wobbles in the Earth's spin, which depend on how near the Moon was, and read that way they say a day then lasted about seventeen hours (*Short days*).

At the start of this stretch the air still held almost no oxygen. Then, about 2.43 billion years ago, the oxygen made by microbes in the sea began to stay in the air (*Oxygen in the air*). For about two hundred million years it came and went, and only by about 2.2 billion years ago was it there for good.
That is what is new: oxygen in the air, for the first time.

How much there was is argued. Even at its highest it was probably well below today's, and near the end there was far less. But a little was enough to change the ground. Iron in rock rusts when oxygen reaches it, and soils and sand began to turn red (*Red rocks*). Many minerals that need oxygen to form could form for the first time.

The oxygen may also have brought the cold. Methane, a gas that kept the Earth warm, is destroyed by oxygen. Ice spread several times in this stretch, and at least once it reached land that lay near the equator (*Great freeze*).
All the life was still microbes. The deep sea still had no oxygen at all.
Seven hundred million years is about as long as the whole Animals line.
Geologists call this stretch the first part of the Proterozoic ("pro-ter-o-ZOH-ik"), Greek for "earlier life". Its three parts have names that mean iron, a stream of lava and a range of mountains.
Near its end, great beds of banded iron were laid down once more, around Lake Superior (*Banded iron*), and most of the land may have come together into one great continent (*Nuna*).

references: Simon Poulton and others, "A 200-million-year delay in permanent atmospheric oxygenation," *Nature*, 2021. Oxygen coming and going, and staying from about 2.22 billion.
Ashley Gumsley and others, "Timing and tempo of the Great Oxidation Event," *PNAS*, 2017. The first rise and the first ice.
Timothy Lyons, Christopher Reinhard and Noah Planavsky, "The rise of oxygen in Earth's early ocean and atmosphere," *Nature*, 2014. How much, and how sure.
Nick Lane, *Oxygen: The Molecule That Made the World* (Oxford University Press, 2002). For a parent.

Big cells.name: Big cells
Big cells.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries fixed by agreement, not by layers of rock (1,800 since 1990; 720 provisional, pending a point in the rock, perhaps at the start of the first snowball, about 717)
Big cells.officialName: no single name: the end of the Paleoproterozoic, the whole Mesoproterozoic, and the Tonian (the middle of the Proterozoic, "earlier life"); some geologists call it the boring billion
Big cells.knownFrom: fossils of single cells and ribbons in shale, mounds built by microbes, and chemistry in the rock
Big cells.insideIt: events *Nuna* (at the start edge), *Cells with nuclei*, *Bangiomorpha*, *Rodinia cracks*. Plots: *Oxygen* (low and flat), *Day length*, *Minerals*.
Big cells.picturesWanted: the ribbon fossils of the Gaoyuzhuang Formation, Hebei (Zhu and others 2016, *Nature Communications*, open access, CC BY; to confirm); *Bangiomorpha* under the microscope (Nicholas Butterfield; licence to ask).
Big cells.summary: A quiet sea for a billion years, with little oxygen and, as far as anyone has found, no ice. In it lived a new kind of cell, bigger than a bacterium, with a nucleus. Some stuck together, and grew long.

more.spanLine: From about 1.8 billion to 720 million years ago.
paragraphs: In the hills of Hebei, in northern China, there is shale that was mud on the floor of a shallow sea about 1.56 billion years ago. Split it open and some layers hold dark ribbons, a few of them as long as a school ruler. Each ribbon was a living thing made of many cells, probably using sunlight like seaweed.

A sea like that would have looked calm. There were no plants on land and no animals, and as far as anyone has found, there was no ice. The air held a little oxygen, how much is argued, and the deep water held none. In places the water stank of rotten eggs. The Moon was closer than now, and a day lasted about eighteen or nineteen hours.

For a long time this stretch seemed so steady that a geologist wrote, in 1995, that never in the Earth's history "did so little happen to so much for so long". It has been called the boring billion. That may be unfair. Oxygen seems to have risen and fallen in pulses, and the continents came together into one (*Nuna*), broke apart, and came together again into another, called Rodinia, which began to crack near the end (*Rodinia cracks*).

What is new is the cell with a nucleus: a cell that keeps its genes in a small bag of their own. Such cells are often ten times as wide as bacteria, and they are the kind that every plant, animal and fungus is made of. The oldest fossils that may be of them are about 1.64 billion years old (*Cells with nuclei*). About 1.05 billion years ago a red seaweed on what is now Somerset Island, in Nunavut, left the oldest signs of sex (*Bangiomorpha*).
A billion years and more is nearly a quarter of the Earth's whole life. It is one and a half times as long as the Animals line.
Geologists have no single name for it. It is the middle of the Proterozoic, "earlier life".
Just after it ended, ice spread from the poles almost to the equator (*Snowball one*).

references: Shixing Zhu and others, "Decimetre-scale multicellular eukaryotes from the 1.56-billion-year-old Gaoyuzhuang Formation in North China," *Nature Communications*, 2016. The scene.

Roger Buick, David Des Marais and Andrew Knoll, "Stable isotopic compositions of carbonates from the Mesoproterozoic Bangemall Group, northwestern Australia," *Chemical Geology*, 1995. "So little… for so long".
Timothy Gibson and others, "Precise age of *Bangiomorpha pubescens* dates the origin of eukaryotic photosynthesis," *Geology*, 2018.
Andrew Knoll, *Life on a Young Planet* (Princeton University Press, 2003). For a parent.

Animals.name: Animals
Animals.spanNote: the start a dated boundary fixed by agreement (the start of the Cryogenian, provisional); moved from a guessed 700 on 10 Oct
Animals.officialName: none for the whole; it starts about 180 million years before the Phanerozoic, Greek for "visible life", which begins 539 million years ago (named by George Chadwick in 1930)
Animals.knownFrom: fossils of animals with hard parts, from about 539 million years ago; before that, rare soft fossils and argued chemistry
Animals.insideIt: every event from *Snowball one* (717) to now: fifty-two, with the two new ones. By line: Soft bodies, ten; Trilobites, twelve; Dinosaurs, seven; Mammals, eleven, and the twelve of batch 6. Plots: *Sea level* (from 540), *Oxygen*, *People* (from 315,000 years ago).
Animals.index: the horse and the elephant line, followed down the Mammals line as events (batch 3)
Animals.picturesWanted: a living sponge, as the animal the oldest argued chemistry points to (Commons; licence to check); a blue whale beside a frond from Mistaken Point, drawn to one scale (to make).
Animals.summary: The first animals were probably small and soft, and left almost nothing behind. Then they grew, a millionfold in a hundred and fifty million years: fronds, trilobites, fish, dinosaurs, whales.

more.spanLine: From about 720 million years ago to now.
paragraphs: At the start of this stretch, ice was about to spread over almost the whole Earth (*Snowball one*). Somewhere in the sea there were probably animals already. Nobody has found them. They were probably small and soft, and they left almost nothing behind.

How can anyone say they were there? From their descendants. Every living animal carries genes copied from its parents, with small changes each time. Counting the differences between the genes of living animals, and how fast such changes pile up, gives a rough date for their common ancestor. The answers run from about 830 to 650 million years ago. In rock in Oman more than 635 million years old there is also a chemical that some scientists read as made by sponges, the simplest animals. Others think algae made it. That is still argued.
What is new is animals: living things made of many cells that eat other living things. Most of them move.

Then they grew. The oldest big fossils that may be animals are about 574 million years old: fronds and quilted shapes on the sea floor, some nearly two metres long (*Mistaken Point*). From about 600 to 450 million years ago the biggest living things became about a million times bigger. Then came trilobites, fish, trees, dinosaurs, and today the blue whale, the heaviest animal known.

The four stretches below are named for what was most noticed in each, not for what arrived first. There were no trilobites at the start of Trilobites, and no dinosaurs at the start of Dinosaurs. Mammals had already lived for about a hundred and forty million years when Mammals began.
Seven hundred and twenty million years is about a sixth of the Earth's whole life.

Geologists have no single name for it. Their Phanerozoic ("fan-er-o-ZOH-ik"), Greek for "visible life", starts later, about 539 million years ago, where fossils of animals with hard parts begin to fill the rocks (*Animals, kept*).
When the first animal lived, and what it looked like, nobody knows.

references: Mario dos Reis and others, "Uncertainty in the timing of origin of animals and the limits of precision in molecular timescales," *Current Biology*, 2015. The gene clocks.
Jonathan Payne and others, "Two-phase increase in the maximum size of life over 3.5 billion years reflects biological innovation and environmental opportunity," *PNAS*, 2009. The millionfold growth.
Douglas Erwin and others, "The Cambrian conundrum: early divergence and later ecological success in the early history of animals," *Science*, 2011. Animals older than their fossils.
Richard Fortey, *Life: An Unauthorised Biography* (HarperCollins, 1997). For a parent.

Soft bodies.name: Soft bodies
Soft bodies.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries: 720 fixed by agreement (provisional); 539 a point in the rock at Fortune Head, Newfoundland, dated 538.8 ± 0.6
Soft bodies.officialName: Cryogenian, "birth of ice", and Ediacaran, after the Ediacara Hills of South Australia, an Aboriginal name whose meaning is argued
Soft bodies.knownFrom: glacial rubble at the equator, and impressions of soft bodies in sandstone and volcanic ash
Soft bodies.insideIt: events *Snowball one*, *Snowball two*, *The thaw*, *Little balls*, *Gaskiers*, *Mistaken Point*, *Charnia*, *Dickinsonia*, *Bites and shells*, *Animals, kept* (at the end edge). Plots: *Oxygen*, *Day length* (about 22 hours at 620).
Soft bodies.picturesWanted: the fronds on the E Surface at Mistaken Point (UNESCO or Parks and Natural Areas, Newfoundland and Labrador; licence to check); a *Dickinsonia* fossil (Commons; licence to check).
Soft bodies.summary: Ice covered nearly the whole Earth, twice. When it melted, big soft things grew on the sea floor: fronds, quilts, discs. Some were animals. None had a shell or a mouth that bit, until the end.

more.spanLine: From about 720 to 539 million years ago.
paragraphs: At Mistaken Point, on the south-eastern tip of Newfoundland, the sea has worn the cliffs away to bare, tilted sheets of rock. On them lie thousands of fossils: fronds like feathers, branched like ferns, some a hand long and some nearly two metres. About 565 million years ago they stood up from the mud of a deep sea floor, where sunlight probably did not reach. Then ash from a volcano settled over them and kept them where they stood (*Mistaken Point*).
Nothing in that scene could bite. None of the fronds had a mouth. Many of them may have fed by soaking up food from the water through their skin.

That is what is new: big living things with soft bodies, the oldest big fossils with complicated shapes. Some, like *Dickinsonia*, an oval quilt up to more than a metre long, were animals: its fossils still hold cholesterol, a fat that is the mark of animals (*Dickinsonia*). What many of the others were, nobody knows.

The stretch began in ice. Twice, ice spread from the poles almost to the equator, first for about fifty-seven million years (*Snowball one*), then for a few million (*Snowball two*). For about a third of this stretch the Earth was white. When the second ice melted, it melted fast (*The thaw*).

Near the end, about 550 million years ago, small animals built tubes of shell. The oldest yet found are in Namibia. In China, some of the tubes have tiny round holes bored through them, the oldest signs yet found of one animal hunting another (*Bites and shells*).
A hundred and eighty million years is a quarter of the Animals line. It is nearly three times as long as everything since the dinosaurs died.

Geologists split this stretch in two. The Cryogenian ("cry-o-JEN-ee-un"), "birth of ice", is the time of the two snowballs. The Ediacaran ("ee-dee-AK-a-run") is named after the Ediacara Hills in South Australia. It was added in 2004, the first new period in more than a hundred years.
At its end, animals with hard parts begin to fill the rocks (*Animals, kept*).

Paul Hoffman and others, "Snowball Earth climate dynamics and Cryogenian geology-geobiology," *Science Advances*, 2017. The two ices.
Mark McMenamin, *The Garden of Ediacara* (Columbia University Press, 1998). For a parent.

Trilobites.name: Trilobites
Trilobites.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries at points in the rock: 538.8 ± 0.6 (Fortune Head, Newfoundland) and 251.902 ± 0.024 (Meishan, Zhejiang)
Trilobites.officialName: Paleozoic, "ancient life"; Adam Sedgwick's word (1838), stretched to this whole span by John Phillips in 1840
Trilobites.knownFrom: fossils of animals and plants with hard parts, in rock laid down in seas, swamps and rivers
Trilobites.opensTo: Shells, Crowded seas, Green land, Fish, Coal forests, One continent
Trilobites.insideIt: events *Animals, kept* (at the start edge), *Chengjiang*, *Burgess Shale*, *The map clears*, *Plants ashore*, *Short, sharp ice*, *Jaws*, *Animals ashore*, *Forests*, *Tiktaalik*, *Land egg*, *Coal*, *The Great Dying* (at the end edge). Plots: *Sea level*, *Oxygen* (the high near 300).
Trilobites.picturesWanted: a trilobite from Chengjiang, legs and all (Yunnan Key Laboratory for Palaeobiology or Commons; licence to check); a trilobite eye, its lenses visible (Commons; licence to check).
Trilobites.summary: The seas filled with animals that had shells, legs and eyes, and among the commonest were trilobites. Then plants and animals came onto the land, and forests grew. At the end, nearly everything died.

more.spanLine: From about 539 to 252 million years ago.
paragraphs: At Chengjiang, in Yunnan, in southern China, there is shale that was mud on the floor of a shallow sea about 518 million years ago. Mud slid over the animals living there and buried them so quickly that their soft parts were kept: legs, guts, eyes. About 250 kinds of animal have been found in it (*Chengjiang*). Many crawled on the sea floor. Some swam above it. Some had claws for catching the others.

Among them, as in rocks of this age all over the world, are trilobites ("TRY-lo-bites"), some of the commonest fossils of the time. A trilobite was an armoured animal with many jointed legs. Most were about the size of a finger; the biggest known was longer than a child's arm. Their eyes had lenses made of a clear mineral, calcite. The lenses were stone even while the animal lived, so they last, and they are among the oldest eyes that can be studied lens by lens. More than twenty thousand kinds have been named.
Yet there were no trilobites at the start of this stretch. The oldest found are about 520 million years old, so for nearly the first twenty million years there were none to find.

What is new is a world of hard parts: shells, spines, jaws, eyes. And, in the middle of the stretch, the land turned green. Plants came ashore (*Plants ashore*), then small animals (*Animals ashore*), then forests (*Forests*), then a fish with fins nearly like legs (*Tiktaalik*), and then eggs that could be laid on dry land (*Land egg*).
Trilobites were most various a little under 500 million years ago and for a while after, and then they dwindled. By the end there were only a few kinds left, small ones.
Two hundred and ninety million years is two fifths of the Animals line. It is longer than the Dinosaurs line and the Mammals line put together.
Geologists call this stretch the Paleozoic ("pay-lee-o-ZOH-ik"), "ancient life".
The last trilobites died in the Great Dying, with four in five kinds of sea animal (*The Great Dying*).

Dinosaurs.name: Dinosaurs
Dinosaurs.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries at points in the rock: 251.902 ± 0.024 (Meishan, Zhejiang) and 66.0 (El Kef, Tunisia)
Dinosaurs.officialName: Mesozoic, "middle life"; named by John Phillips in 1840
Dinosaurs.knownFrom: fossils in rock laid down on land and in shallow seas, and the seafloor's magnetic stripes from about 200 million years ago
Dinosaurs.insideIt: events *The Great Dying* (at the start edge), *Lystrosaurus* (new, below), *Dinosaurs*, *Pangaea cracks*, *Triassic ends*, *Archaeopteryx*, *Flowers*, *The asteroid* (at the end edge). Plots: *Sea level* (high in the Cretaceous), *Oxygen*.
Dinosaurs.picturesWanted: a *Lystrosaurus* skeleton (Iziko South African Museum or Commons; licence to check); a map of Pangaea at 250 million years (our own map, at that year).
Dinosaurs.summary: After the Great Dying, the one great continent was hot and nearly empty. For millions of years it filled slowly. Dinosaurs arrived about twenty million years in, and ruled the land for most of the rest.

more.spanLine: From about 252 to 66 million years ago.
paragraphs: In the Karoo of South Africa, a dry country of flat-topped hills, there are layers of old river mud from just after the Great Dying. Nine in ten of the bones found in them belong to one animal: *Lystrosaurus* ("liss-tro-SAW-rus"), a stocky plant-eater about a metre long, with two tusks and a beak (*Lystrosaurus*).

That emptiness is the scene. All the land was joined in one continent, Pangaea, and much of its middle was desert. In the tropics the sea at the surface may have been as hot as a hot bath, about 40 °C, and for about five million years almost no fish or reptiles lived there. It took eight or nine million years for the living world to fill up again.

There were no dinosaurs in it. The oldest found, in Brazil and Argentina, are about 233 to 231 million years old, nearly twenty million years after this stretch began (*Dinosaurs*). Even then they were not in charge. For a long time the reptiles on the crocodile side of the family were often more common and came in more shapes.

Then, about 201 million years ago, Pangaea began to crack open, volcanoes poured out lava along the cracks, and another dying took away many of those rivals (*Pangaea cracks*, *Triassic ends*). After it, dinosaurs ruled the land.

What is new is the dinosaurs, and the world they lived in: for most of this stretch the Earth was warm, with little or no ice at the poles. Birds appeared (*Archaeopteryx*), and so did flowers (*Flowers*). Small mammals lived through most of it.
A hundred and eighty-six million years is a quarter of the Animals line. It is nearly three times as long as the Mammals line.
Geologists call this stretch the Mesozoic ("mez-o-ZOH-ik"), "middle life". John Phillips, an English geologist, gave it the name in 1840.
It ended about 66 million years ago, when an asteroid about ten kilometres across hit what is now Yucatán, in Mexico, and every dinosaur died except the birds (*The asteroid*).

more.spanLine: From about 66 million years ago to now.
paragraphs: At Corral Bluffs, in Colorado, the rock holds the first million years after the asteroid, layer on layer. Just above the layer of the impact, the rock is suddenly full of fern spores (*Fern spike*). The biggest mammals that lived through the impact there weighed about half a kilogram, the size of a rat. Within about a hundred thousand years there were palm forests, and mammals the size of raccoons. Within about three hundred thousand, some weighed as much as a big dog. By seven hundred thousand years there were beans, and mammals the size of wolves.
That is what is new: mammals got big.

Mammals themselves were old. The oldest ones known, small animals like shrews, lived about 140 million years before this stretch began. Through the whole age of dinosaurs most mammals stayed small. So mammals had lived more than twice as long before this stretch as they have lived in it.

Later in the stretch, the Earth went through a sudden heat (*Hot spike*), then a long cooling, with ice settling on Antarctica (*Antarctica freezes*). Grass spread over the plains (*Grasslands*), and near the end, ice came and went across the north again and again (*Ice by turns*).
Sixty-six million years is about a tenth of the Animals line. Trilobites lasted more than four times as long.
Geologists call this stretch the Cenozoic ("see-no-ZOH-ik"), "new life". John Phillips, an English geologist, gave it the name in 1840.
The name marks the animals that grew large on land. It does not mean the dinosaurs had gone. Birds are dinosaurs, and there are more kinds of bird alive today than of mammal.

more.spanLine: From about 539 to 487 million years ago.
paragraphs: In the Flinders Ranges of South Australia, near an old mine called Ajax, there is grey limestone that was once a reef in a warm, shallow sea, about 520 million years ago. The rock is full of small cups and cones, most of them a few centimetres across, each with a double wall full of holes. They were archaeocyaths ("AR-kee-oh-SIGH-aths"), animals that were probably sponges. Growing together with microbes that also made lime, they built mounds of rock on the sea floor: some of the first big reefs built partly by animals.

Around reefs like these, and on sea floors everywhere, lived animals with hard parts. That is what is new: shells, spines and armour, and eyes too, not in a few kinds of animal but in thousands. A few animals had made shells before (*Bites and shells*). Now hard parts were everywhere, and because hard parts last, the rocks fill with fossils (*Animals, kept*).

Within about twenty million years, fossils turn up of most of the great branches of the animal family alive today: animals with jointed legs, animals with shells in two halves, snails, worms, and the branch with a stiff rod along the back, the one fish belong to. In a few places mud buried animals so fast that their soft parts were kept as well (*Chengjiang*, *Burgess Shale*).

Most of the land lay south of the equator, much of it joined in one great continent, Gondwana (*The map clears*). The sea was warm, and it rose through the stretch. The air held less oxygen than it does now.
Fifty-two million years is nearly four fifths as long as the whole Mammals line.

Geologists call this stretch the Cambrian ("KAM-bree-un"), from Cambria, the name for Wales in medieval Latin, where Adam Sedgwick, an English geologist, studied its rocks. He gave it the name in 1835.
At its end the sea was full of animals. On land, as far as anyone can tell, nothing grew but films of microbes.

more.spanLine: From about 487 to 444 million years ago.
paragraphs: In and around Cincinnati, in Ohio, the hillsides and creek beds are made of thin grey layers of limestone and mud, and much of the limestone is nothing but shells. About 450 million years ago this was the floor of a warm, shallow sea, south of the equator, in a belt of storms. The storms heaped the shells into beds.

Pick up a slab and there are shells in two halves, from fingernail to coin size; little stony twigs and crusts that were colonies of tiny animals; stems of sea lilies, animals related to starfish that stood on stalks; and trilobites. One trilobite, *Isotelus* ("eye-so-TEE-lus"), grew longer than a hand. Hunting over the sea floor were animals with long, straight, pointed shells, relatives of the nautilus, the octopus and the squid. The biggest piece of such a shell ever found is three metres long, and it is only part of a shell.
That is what is new: how many kinds of animal there were. In about twenty-five million years the number of kinds of sea animal grew three or four times over. Trilobites came in more shapes than ever.

The seas themselves spread. Sea level stood higher than at almost any other time we know of, perhaps a hundred and fifty metres above today's, and by some estimates more than two hundred, and shallow seas covered much of the continents.

On land, about 470 million years ago, plants left spores in rock in what is now Argentina, the oldest sign of plants on land that most specialists accept (*Plants ashore*). The plants themselves have never been found.
Forty-three million years is about two thirds as long as the Mammals line.

Geologists call this stretch the Ordovician ("or-duh-VISH-un"), after the Ordovices, a people who lived in north Wales when the Romans came. Charles Lapworth, an English geologist, gave it the name in 1879.
At its end, ice spread over what is now North Africa, which then lay near the South Pole, and the seas grew cold. Most kinds of sea animal died out (*Short, sharp ice*).

more.spanLine: From about 444 to 419 million years ago.
paragraphs: At Perton, near Stoke Edith, in Herefordshire, close to the border with Wales, there is rock from near the end of this stretch, laid down where rivers ran into the sea. A plant from it is called *Cooksonia* ("cook-SOH-nee-a"), after Isabel Cookson, the Australian botanist who collected it.

*Cooksonia* was a few centimetres tall. It had no leaves and no flowers: only thin green stems that forked, and forked again, with a small round case at the tip of each branch, full of spores. A bank covered in it would have been green, and none of it taller than a finger.

That is what is new: plants that stood up. Plants had been on land for some forty million years already (*Plants ashore*), but as far as anyone knows they lay low and flat, like liverworts. To stand up, a plant needs stiff stems, with pipes inside to carry water up from the ground. Some fossils of *Cooksonia* show such pipes.

The stretch began just after the great ice had shrunk, when most kinds of sea animal had died (*Short, sharp ice*). The seas grew warm again and stood high. Fish with jaws spread through them (*Jaws*), and sea scorpions, some of them about two metres long, hunted in the shallows.
Small animals came onto the land. The oldest one known to have breathed air was like a little millipede, from Stonehaven, in Scotland, though its age is argued (*Animals ashore*).

The tallest living thing on land was not a plant but *Prototaxites* ("pro-toe-tax-EYE-teez"), most likely a fungus: a trunk with no branches. The biggest found, a little younger than this stretch, stood about eight metres tall.
Twenty-five million years is a little over a third as long as the Mammals line.

Geologists call it the Silurian ("sigh-LOOR-ee-un"), after the Silures, a people who lived in south-east Wales when the Romans came. Roderick Murchison, a Scottish geologist, gave it the name in 1835.

more.spanLine: From about 419 to 359 million years ago.
paragraphs: In the Kimberley, in the far north of Western Australia, a line of limestone hills was once a reef in a warm sea, about 380 million years ago. Beside the reef the water was deep and still, with little oxygen. Dead fish sank into it and were sealed in lumps of lime before they could rot. Today, when collectors soak those lumps in weak acid, the same acid that is in vinegar, the fish come out whole, every bone in place.

Many of the Gogo fish were placoderms ("PLAK-o-derms"), fish whose heads and chests were covered in plates of bone, with sharp-edged plates of bone in their jaws. One, named *Materpiscis*, "mother fish", has a young one inside her, still joined by its cord: one of the oldest known animals with backbones to give birth to live young.

That is what is new: fish of every shape. Armoured fish, sharks, fish with thin rays in their fins like most fish today, and fish with fleshy fins built on bones. The biggest of the armoured fish, *Dunkleosteus*, was about three or four metres long.

Fish were not new. Fish with jaws are known from about 439 million years ago (*Jaws*), and fish without jaws from long before. The name marks the time when fish were the most noticed animals, not when they began.

The oldest forest yet found grew where Somerset is now, about 390 million years ago (*Forests*), and by the end of the stretch there were trees with wood and leaves in many places. In rivers lived fish with necks and bony fins (*Tiktaalik*).
A year then had about four hundred days, as fossil corals count them.
Sixty million years is nearly as long as the whole Mammals line.
Geologists call this stretch the Devonian ("di-VOH-nee-un"), after Devon, in England. Adam Sedgwick and Roderick Murchison gave it the name in 1839.
It ended in a long run of dyings. Reefs like the one at Gogo were among the worst hit, and by the end every armoured fish was gone.

more.spanLine: From about 359 to 299 million years ago.
paragraphs: Stand in a coal swamp near the end of this stretch and the trees are like nothing alive. The tallest are scale trees: bare poles thirty metres high or more, a metre or more thick at the base, with a crown of branches only at the very top. Their bark is covered in diamond-shaped scars where leaves once grew. Their nearest relatives alive today are small plants called quillworts.

Over the water flies *Meganeura* ("meg-a-NEW-ra"), its wings about seventy centimetres across. Its fossils come from coal mines at Commentry, in France. It looked like a dragonfly, but it belonged to a group of insects that is now gone, sometimes called griffinflies. On the forest floor lived *Arthropleura*, a millipede that grew to more than two and a half metres long.

That is what is new: forests so wide and so wet that their dead plants piled up faster than they could rot, and were buried, and became coal (*Coal*). The swamps grew in a belt along the equator, where the continents were coming together into one.
The air held more oxygen than it does now: at least a quarter as much again, and perhaps more (*Oxygen*).
Near the South Pole, ice sheets grew and melted many times. Each time the sea fell and rose, so layers of swamp and layers of sea lie stacked one on another.

Animals with backbones walked the land. Clawed footprints about 355 million years old, in Victoria, Australia, may have been made by animals whose eggs could be laid on dry land. By about 315 million years ago, small animals like lizards were trapped in hollow tree stumps in Nova Scotia (*Land egg*).
About 305 million years ago the climate grew drier, and the great swamp forests broke apart into patches.
Sixty million years is nearly as long as the whole Mammals line.
Geologists call this stretch the Carboniferous ("kar-buh-NIF-er-us"), "coal-bearing". William Conybeare and William Phillips, two English geologists, gave it the name in 1822.

more.spanLine: From about 299 to 252 million years ago.
paragraphs: In the ranch country around Seymour, in north Texas, the ground is red: old river mud and old soil, stained by rusted iron. About 280 million years ago rivers wound through it to ponds, with ferns by the water and conifers on the drier ground. In the ponds lived a fresh-water shark and *Diplocaulus*, an amphibian with a head shaped like a boomerang. Along the banks walked *Dimetrodon*, three metres long, with a tall sail on its back (*Dimetrodon*).
*Dimetrodon* was not a dinosaur. It died out about forty million years before the oldest dinosaurs yet found. It was not a reptile either. It belonged to the same great branch of animals as mammals.

What is new is one continent. Through the stretch before, the continents had been coming together, and now nearly all the land was joined, from near the South Pole to far into the north, in one great continent, Pangaea ("pan-JEE-a"), Greek for "all the Earth". Its middle was far from any sea. Much of it was dry, with deserts in many places and great rains in their season. The ice near the South Pole melted away early in the stretch.

On land, most of the largest animals were on the mammals' branch: first sail-backs like *Dimetrodon*, and later animals with sabre teeth, and plant-eaters with tusks and beaks. In the south grew forests of a tree called *Glossopteris*. Its fossil leaves, found in Africa, India, South America, Australia and Antarctica, helped show, long afterwards, that those lands had once been joined.
Forty-seven million years is about seven tenths as long as the Mammals line.
Geologists call this stretch the Permian ("PUR-mee-un"), after Perm, an old province of Russia west of the Ural Mountains, where Roderick Murchison studied its rocks. He gave it the name in 1841.
It ended in the Great Dying, when four in five kinds of sea animal died out, probably because of volcanoes in Siberia (*The Great Dying*).

more.spanLine: From about 252 to 201 million years ago.
paragraphs: At Ghost Ranch, in northern New Mexico, there is a quarry where in 1947 a museum team found a bed of dinosaur bones, skeleton lying on skeleton: hundreds of them, perhaps more than a thousand animals. All are *Coelophysis* ("see-lo-FY-sis"), a slender hunter up to three metres long, most of it neck and tail, about as heavy as a middle-sized dog. How so many died together is argued; a flood is the leading guess. They lived late in this stretch, perhaps 205 million years ago.

They were late. For nearly the first twenty million years of this stretch there were no dinosaurs at all (*Dinosaurs*). Even after the dinosaurs appeared, they were few. The crocodile side of the reptile family was commoner and came in more shapes: long-snouted fish-eaters, armoured plant-eaters, big hunters that walked upright.
What is new is a crowd of new kinds of animal, and many of their families are still alive: the oldest turtles, the oldest flying reptiles, small animals very close to the mammals, and the dinosaurs.

The stretch began in an emptied world, just after the Great Dying, when one plant-eater, *Lystrosaurus*, was by far the commonest animal in many places (*Lystrosaurus*). All the land was one continent, Pangaea. Its middle was hot and dry, and there was no ice at either pole. About 233 million years ago, rain fell hard, on and off, for about two million years.
Fifty-one million years is more than a quarter of the Dinosaurs line, and about three quarters as long as the Mammals line.

Geologists call this stretch the Triassic ("try-ASS-ik"), "threefold", for three layers of rock that lie one on another in Germany: a coloured sandstone, a limestone full of shells, and coloured clays. Friedrich von Alberti, a German geologist, gave it the name in 1834.

It ended about 201 million years ago, when Pangaea began to crack and lava poured out along the cracks (*Pangaea cracks*). The big relatives of crocodiles died. The dinosaurs lived on (*Triassic ends*).

Giants.summary: Dinosaurs ruled the land, and the long-necked plant-eaters grew into some of the largest animals that ever walked. Pangaea split, and a narrow Atlantic opened. *Archaeopteryx* flew on feathered wings.

more.spanLine: From about 201 to 143 million years ago.
paragraphs: At Dinosaur National Monument, in Utah, a hall has been built against a wall of tilted sandstone. In the wall are about fifteen hundred dinosaur bones, left where they lie: backbones, ribs, leg bones, a skull here and there. About 150 million years ago this was a river. Animals died in dry years, and floods washed their bones onto a sandbar and buried them.

Earl Douglass, of the Carnegie Museum, found the first of them in 1909: eight bones of a tail, sticking out of the rock. Most of the bones are from long-necked plant-eaters, *Apatosaurus*, *Diplodocus* and *Camarasaurus*. With them are *Stegosaurus*, with plates along its back, and *Allosaurus*, a hunter.

That is what is new: giants. The long-necked dinosaurs, called sauropods ("SORE-o-pods"), grew longer and heavier than any land animal before them. Some in this stretch were more than twenty-five metres long and weighed as much as several elephants. The very largest came later (*Flowers*).

The dinosaurs took over the land at the start, after a dying that took many of their rivals (*Triassic ends*). In eastern North America, footprints of big meat-eating dinosaurs appear in the rock within ten thousand years (*Big footprints*).

Pangaea came apart. North America pulled away from Africa, and between them a narrow Atlantic Ocean opened. The world was warm, with no ice at the poles. Late in the stretch, on islands in a warm sea where Bavaria is now, lived *Archaeopteryx*, an animal with feathered wings, teeth and a long bony tail (*Archaeopteryx*).
Fifty-eight million years is nearly a third of the Dinosaurs line.

Geologists call this stretch the Jurassic ("joo-RASS-ik"), after the Jura Mountains, on the border of France and Switzerland. Alexander von Humboldt named the limestone of the Jura in 1799, and Alexandre Brongniart, a French geologist, made it the name of a stretch of time in 1829.
Where this stretch ends has not yet been tied to a layer of rock anywhere in the world.

Kim Cohen, David Harper, Philip Gibbard and Nicholas Car, "The ICS International Chronostratigraphic Chart this decade," *Episodes*, 2025. The new end date.
Paul Olsen and others, "Ascent of dinosaurs linked to an iridium anomaly at the Triassic-Jurassic boundary," *Science*, 2002.

Flowers.name: Flowers
Flowers.spanNote: the start a boundary fixed by agreement, 143.1 ± 0.6, with no point in the rock yet (moved from 145, Michael, 10 Oct); the end a dated boundary at a point in the rock, 66.0 (El Kef, Tunisia)
Flowers.officialName: Cretaceous, "chalky", from the Latin *creta*, chalk; named by Jean-Baptiste-Julien d'Omalius d'Halloy in 1822, for the chalk of the Paris Basin
Flowers.knownFrom: chalk, bones, leaves and pollen, amber, and the ocean floor
Flowers.insideIt: events *Oldest flowers* (renamed from *Flowers*), *The asteroid* (at the end edge). Plots: *Sea level* (the high between about 90 and 80), *Oxygen*.
Flowers.picturesWanted: the White Cliffs of Dover (Commons; licence to check); coccoliths under an electron microscope (Commons or NHM; licence to check).
Flowers.summary: A warm world, with seas high over the land, laying down chalk. Flowering plants appeared and spread, until by the end they were the most varied plants in much of the world. *Tyrannosaurus* lived at the very end.

more.spanLine: From about 143 to 66 million years ago.
paragraphs: The White Cliffs of Dover stand more than a hundred metres over the sea between England and France. They are chalk, and chalk under a microscope is mostly tiny plates of lime, each a few thousandths of a millimetre across. The plates were the armour of single-celled algae called coccolithophores ("cock-o-LITH-o-fores"). When the algae died, their plates sank, and settled on the sea floor, about a centimetre every thousand years, until the chalk was hundreds of metres thick. The cliffs east of Dover are about 94 to 86 million years old.

For the sea floor to be where Dover is, the sea had to be high. At their highest, shallow seas covered about a third of today's land, and one cut North America in two. Between about 90 and 80 million years ago, guesses for the height of the sea run from about fifty metres above today's to more than two hundred (*Sea level*). The world was warm, with no large ice sheets for most of the stretch.

What is new is flowers. Pollen of flowering plants goes back about 135 million years. Among the oldest whole flowering plants yet found are water plants with no petals, about 125 million years old (*Oldest flowers*). By the end of the stretch, flowering plants were the most varied plants in much of the world, though conifers and ferns still made up much of many forests.

The dinosaurs went on, and some grew larger than ever. *Argentinosaurus*, from about 95 million years ago, was perhaps thirty-five metres long, among the largest animals ever to walk. At the very end lived *Tyrannosaurus* and *Triceratops*.
Seventy-seven million years is longer than the whole Mammals line.

Geologists call this stretch the Cretaceous ("kri-TAY-shus"), "chalky", from *creta*, the Latin word for chalk. Jean-Baptiste d'Omalius d'Halloy, a Belgian geologist, gave it the name in 1822, for the chalk around Paris.
It ended about 66 million years ago, when an asteroid about ten kilometres across hit what is now Yucatán, in Mexico (*The asteroid*).

references: Kenneth Miller and others, "The Phanerozoic record of global sea-level change," *Science*, 2005.
Bernard Gomez and others, "*Montsechia*, an ancient aquatic angiosperm," *PNAS*, 2015.

Thomas Henry Huxley, "On a Piece of Chalk" (1868; free online). For a parent.

Recovery.name: Recovery
Recovery.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries at points in the rock: 66.00 (El Kef, Tunisia) and 56.00 (Dababiya, near Luxor, Egypt)
Recovery.officialName: Paleocene, "the old part of the Eocene", from Greek *palaios*, old; named by Wilhelm Philipp Schimper in 1874
Recovery.knownFrom: fossil leaves, pollen and bones in rock laid down by rivers and swamps, and shells in seafloor mud
Recovery.insideIt: events *The asteroid* (at the start edge), *Fern spike* (at the start edge), *Hot spike* (at the end edge). Plots: *Sea level*, *Oxygen*.
Recovery.index: the elephant line begins: *Eritherium*, about 60 million years ago in Morocco, about 5 kilograms, the size of a large cat. No horse yet.
Recovery.picturesWanted: a giant fossil leaf from Cerrejón (Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute or Florida Museum; licence to ask); a *Titanoboa* vertebra beside a modern anaconda's (Florida Museum; licence to ask).
Recovery.summary: Forests grew back, and a warm, wet world filled up again. Mammals were growing, but in the tropics the giants were still reptiles: crocodiles, turtles, and a snake as long as a bus.

more.spanLine: From about 66 to 56 million years ago.
paragraphs: In La Guajira, in the far north of Colombia, the homeland of the Wayuu people, there is a coal mine, one of the biggest in the world. The coal was once a swamp. In the rock between the seams of coal lie thousands of fossil leaves, many of them big, from a forest that grew there about 58 million years ago. They are the oldest rainforest leaves found in the tropics of the Americas. The trees belong to families that still grow in rainforests today: palms, beans, the avocado's family, the banana's.

That forest was hot and wet, hotter than the same place is now, with more than two and a half metres of rain a year. In its rivers lived crocodile cousins, big turtles, and a snake about thirteen metres long, called *Titanoboa* ("TY-tan-o-BO-a"), the biggest snake known. No mammal has been reported there.

That is what is new: forests and their animals, built again after the asteroid (*The asteroid*). Just after the impact, ferns had covered the ground (*Fern spike*). By about 58 million years ago, as Cerrejón shows, there was rainforest near the equator again.

Mammals were growing, though not yet big. At Corral Bluffs, in Colorado, the biggest weighed about half a kilogram just after the impact, and about fifty kilograms, the size of a wolf, seven hundred thousand years later. By the end of this stretch a few plant-eaters were as heavy as a cow. In Morocco, about 60 million years ago, lived *Eritherium*, the size of a large cat, the oldest animal known of the elephant line.
The world was warm all over, with no ice sheets at the poles.
Ten million years is about a seventh of the Mammals line. It is nearly twice as long as the whole Ice line.

Geologists call this stretch the Paleocene ("PAY-lee-o-seen"). Wilhelm Schimper, who studied fossil plants, gave it the name in 1874. It means "the old part of the Eocene", the stretch that comes next.
It ended in a sudden heat (*Hot spike*).

Jason Head and others, "Giant boid snake from the Palaeocene neotropics reveals hotter past equatorial temperatures," *Nature*, 2009. *Titanoboa*.

Heat.name: Heat
Heat.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries at points in the rock: 56.00 (Dababiya, near Luxor, Egypt) and 33.9 (Massignano, near Ancona, Italy)
Heat.officialName: Eocene, "dawn of the recent", from Greek *eos*, dawn, and *kainos*, new; published by Charles Lyell in 1833, from a name William Whewell suggested
Heat.knownFrom: fossils of plants and animals far north of where their kind lives now, and the chemistry of shells in seafloor mud
Heat.insideIt: events *Hot spike* (at the start edge), *Antarctica freezes* (at the end edge). Plots: *Sea level*, *Oxygen*.
Heat.index: the horse begins: *Sifrhippus*, at the very start, in the Bighorn Basin of Wyoming, about 5.5 kilograms, the size of a cat, shrinking to about 4 during the *Hot spike*. The elephant line: *Moeritherium*, near the end, in the Fayum of Egypt, about 235 kilograms, the size of a big pig.
Heat.picturesWanted: the fossil forest stumps of Axel Heiberg Island, or the Strathcona Fiord beds on Ellesmere (Geological Survey of Canada or Carnegie Museum; licence to ask); a living dawn redwood (Commons; licence to check).
Heat.summary: The warmest world since the dinosaurs died. For most of it there were no ice sheets anywhere. Forests grew in the far north of Canada, with alligators, giant tortoises and tapirs living among the trees.

more.spanLine: From about 56 to 34 million years ago.
paragraphs: On Ellesmere Island, in Nunavut, in the far north of Canada, the ground is bare rock and snow for most of the year, and winter is months of darkness at about forty below. In that rock lie the stumps and leaves of a swamp forest that grew there about 52 million years ago. Most of its trees were dawn redwoods, a kind that still grows wild in China. Among their roots lived alligators, giant tortoises, monitor lizards and tapirs.
The island stood almost as far north then as it does now. Its winters were still dark, for about four months at a time. But they were mild, near freezing, and the summers were warm.

That is what is new: heat. The stretch began with a sudden jump in warmth (*Hot spike*). About 50 million years ago the Earth stayed hotter, for longer, than at any time since the dinosaurs died. The average temperature of the whole surface was perhaps 27 degrees; today it is about 15. For most of this stretch there were no ice sheets anywhere.

Mammals filled the forests. In Wyoming, at the very start of the stretch, lived *Sifrhippus*, one of the oldest horses known, about the size of a cat. In Egypt, near the end, lived *Moeritherium* ("meer-ee-THEER-ee-um"), an animal of the elephant line, the size of a big pig, with a long body and short legs.
After about 50 million years ago, the Earth slowly cooled.
Twenty-two million years is a third of the Mammals line. It is about four times as long as the Ice line.

Geologists call this stretch the Eocene ("EE-o-seen"), Greek for "dawn of the recent". Charles Lyell, a Scottish geologist, published the name in 1833. He sorted rocks by how many of their fossil shells belong to kinds still alive. In rocks of this age, only a few do.
It ended when ice began to stay on Antarctica (*Antarctica freezes*).

Cooling.name: Cooling
Cooling.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries at points in the rock: 33.9 (Massignano, near Ancona, Italy) and 23.04 (Lemme-Carrosio, Piedmont, Italy); the chart moved the second from 23.03 to 23.04 in v2024/12

Cooling.knownFrom: bones in old river mud and ash on the Great Plains, and the chemistry of shells in seafloor mud, which records the ice
Cooling.insideIt: events *Antarctica freezes* (at the start edge). Plots: *Sea level* (the fall at about 34 million years), *Oxygen*.
Cooling.index: the horse: *Mesohippus*, with three toes, about 60 centimetres at the shoulder, the size of a greyhound. The elephant line: *Phiomia*, in the Fayum of Egypt, about 1,200 kilograms.
Cooling.picturesWanted: the striped walls of the Badlands, South Dakota (National Park Service, public domain); a *Mesohippus* skeleton (Commons or the South Dakota School of Mines museum; licence to check).
Cooling.summary: Ice settled on Antarctica and stayed. The world grew cooler and drier, the sea fell, and in many places thick forest thinned to open woodland. In it lived horses with three toes.

more.spanLine: From about 34 to 23 million years ago.
paragraphs: In South Dakota there is a country of steep, striped hills and gullies that the Lakota call *mako sica*, "bad lands". The stripes are layers of mud and ash laid down by rivers. The lower layers, a little older than this stretch, hold the bones of alligators and of big animals that lived in wet forest. The layers just above them, from about 34 to 30 million years ago, hold the bones of animals of open woodland: small horses called *Mesohippus* ("mez-o-HIP-us"), with three toes on each foot and about as tall as a greyhound, and plant-eaters called oreodonts, as common there as zebras are on the Serengeti today.

That change in the rock is the change in the world. It began when an ice sheet grew across East Antarctica, over a few hundred thousand years, and the sea fell by about fifty-five to seventy metres (*Antarctica freezes*). There has been ice on Antarctica ever since.
That is what is new: a cold pole. As ice grew at one end of the Earth, the whole Earth grew cooler, and in many places drier.

Some animals were enormous. In Asia lived *Paraceratherium* ("para-sera-THEER-ee-um"), a hornless cousin of the rhinoceros, nearly five metres tall at the shoulder, one of the biggest land mammals ever found. In Egypt, animals of the elephant line had grown heavier than a cow.
Eleven million years is a sixth of the Mammals line. It is about twice as long as the Ice line.

Geologists call this stretch the Oligocene ("OL-i-go-seen"), Greek for "few of the recent". Its rocks hold a few more shells of kinds still alive than older rocks do. Heinrich Ernst Beyrich, a German geologist, gave it the name in 1854.
In the Badlands, rain wears the hills back a little every year, and new bones come out of the layers.

Felisa Smith and others, "The evolution of maximum body size of terrestrial mammals," *Science*, 2010. *Paraceratherium* and the growth of mammals.
National Park Service, "Geologic Formations: How Badlands Buttes Came to Be," Badlands National Park. The layers.
Stephen Brusatte, *The Rise and Reign of the Mammals* (Mariner Books, 2022). For a parent.

Grass.name: Grass
Grass.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries at points in the rock: 23.04 (Lemme-Carrosio, Piedmont, Italy) and 5.333 (Eraclea Minoa, Sicily)
Grass.officialName: Miocene, "less recent", from Greek *meion*, less, and *kainos*, new; published by Charles Lyell in 1833
Grass.knownFrom: bones and grass husks in volcanic ash and river sand, tiny pieces of glass that grasses leave in old soils, and the teeth of animals that ate grass
Grass.index: the horse: at Ashfall, five kinds of horse, some with three toes and some with one, with tall-crowned teeth for grass. The elephant line: giants, among them *Deinotherium*, up to about 4 metres at the shoulder and perhaps 10 tonnes.
Grass.picturesWanted: the rhino skeletons in the Hubbard Rhino Barn at Ashfall Fossil Beds (University of Nebraska State Museum; licence to ask); a *Deinotherium* skull with its downturned tusks (Commons; licence to check).
Grass.summary: Grass spread over open country, in some places and then in more. Horses grew taller teeth to grind it. Late in the stretch, grasses that like heat and sun covered much of the warm world.

more.spanLine: From about 23 to 5.3 million years ago.
paragraphs: In Nebraska, near the village of Royal, there is a barn built over a hole in the ground. In the hole lie the skeletons of rhinos, horses and camels, whole, as they died about 12 million years ago at a waterhole. A volcano more than a thousand kilometres away, in what is now Idaho, had erupted, and the wind carried its ash across the plains. The ash drifted into the waterhole until it lay two or three metres deep. The animals breathed it in and died over days and weeks: the birds first, then the horses and camels, and the rhinos last, after about a month.
Some of the rhinos have grass seeds in their mouths and among their ribs, from what they ate last.

That is what is new: grass, enough of it to cover open country. The oldest grasslands yet found in North America are about 22 million years old (*Grasslands*). Grass, and the grit on it, is hard on teeth, and over this stretch many grass-eaters grew teeth with tall crowns, which take longer to wear down. At the waterhole lived five kinds of horse, some with three toes and some with one.

The world was warm at first, warmest about 16 million years ago, and then it cooled. Late in the stretch, grasses that grow best in hot, bright, dry places spread over much of the warmer part of the world (*Hot-country grasses*). In what is now the desert of northern Chad, about 7 million years ago, lived an ape that may have walked upright (*Walking upright*).
The elephant line had giants. *Deinotherium* ("dine-o-THEER-ee-um"), with tusks that curved down from its lower jaw, stood up to about four metres at the shoulder.
Nearly eighteen million years is about a quarter of the Mammals line.

Geologists call this stretch the Miocene ("MY-o-seen"), Greek for "less recent". Charles Lyell published the name in 1833. Fewer of the fossil shells in its rocks are of kinds still alive than in the rocks above it.
Under the barn, some of the rhino mothers still carry their unborn young.

Ice.name: Ice
Ice.spanNote: the start a dated boundary at a point in the rock: 5.333 (Eraclea Minoa, Sicily)
Ice.officialName: three: the Pliocene, "more recent" (Charles Lyell, 1833); the Pleistocene, "most recent" (Lyell, 1839); and the Holocene, "wholly recent" (Paul Gervais, 1867–69). The last two together are the Quaternary, "fourth".
Ice.knownFrom: shells in seafloor mud, which record the ice; bones and tools in the rift valleys of East Africa; frozen ground; and, at the end, ice cores
Ice.insideIt: events *Stone tools*, *Lucy* (new, below), *Panama closes*, *Ice by turns*, *Homo sapiens*, the twelve of batch 6 (*Shell beads* to *Altamira*), *Last glacial maximum*, *Ice lets go*, and the events of After the Ice. Plots: *Sea level*, *Oxygen*, *People* (from 315,000 years ago).
Ice.index: the horse: *Equus*, the kind alive today, by about 4 million years ago; the Hagerman horses of Idaho, about 4 to 3 million years old, were like zebras. The elephant line: mammoths, out of Africa into Europe and Asia by about 3 million years ago.
Ice.picturesWanted: Kap København today, the bare hills by the frozen sea (Natural History Museum of Denmark; licence to ask); a painting of the Kap København forest with mastodons (Beth Zaiken's artwork for the 2022 paper; licence to ask).
Ice.summary: The north froze, then thawed, then froze again, about fifty times. Each cold spell grew ice sheets over the north of the world. The last one ended about 11,700 years ago, and the ice has not come back.

more.spanLine: From about 5.3 million years ago to now.
paragraphs: At Kap København, at the top of Greenland, the ground is bare and frozen, and the sea beside it is frozen much of the year. About two million years ago, a forest of poplar, birch and thuja trees grew there. The wood and leaves are gone, but tiny pieces of the genes of things that lived there are still in the mud. A team led by Kurt Kjær and Eske Willerslev read them in 2022. They are the oldest genes yet read. They tell of mastodons, cousins of the elephants, and of reindeer, hares and geese, in a place more than ten degrees warmer than it is now.

At the start of this stretch the whole world was warmer than now, and the sea stood higher. About 2.7 million years ago, ice sheets began to grow over the far north. From about 2.6 million years ago they grew and melted away again, over and over (*Ice by turns*).

That is what is new: ice that comes and goes. At first the ice came and went about every forty thousand years. In the last million years, about every hundred thousand. Each time, the warm spell was the shorter part.

Much else happened. North and South America were joined at Panama (*Panama closes*). In Africa, someone made the oldest stone tools yet found (*Stone tools*), and much later lived the oldest people yet found of our own species (*Homo sapiens*). Horses of the kind alive today appeared, and mammoths walked out of Africa into Europe and Asia.
Five million three hundred thousand years is about a twelfth of the Mammals line. The three stretches below it, *Lucy*, *Hand axes* and *Mammoths*, are each shorter than the one before.

Geologists split this stretch three ways: the Pliocene ("PLY-o-seen"), Greek for "more recent"; the Pleistocene ("PLY-sto-seen"), "most recent"; and the last 11,700 years, the Holocene ("HOL-o-seen"), "wholly recent". Charles Lyell named the first two, in 1833 and 1839.
The last cold spell ended about 11,700 years ago (*Ice lets go*), and the ice has not come back.

Gerald Haug and others, "North Pacific seasonality and the glaciation of North America 2.7 million years ago," *Nature*, 2005. The first northern ice.

Lucy.name: Lucy
Lucy.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries at points in the rock: 5.333 (Eraclea Minoa, Sicily) and 2.58 (Monte San Nicola, near Gela, Sicily)
Lucy.officialName: Pliocene, "more recent", from Greek *pleion*, more, and *kainos*, new; published by Charles Lyell in 1833. Its end was moved from 1.8 to 2.58 million years ago in 2009.
Lucy.knownFrom: bones and footprints in volcanic ash and lake mud in the rift valleys of East Africa, and shells in seafloor mud
Lucy.insideIt: events *Stone tools*, *Lucy* (new, below), *Panama closes*, *Ice by turns* (at the end edge). Plots: *Sea level*, *Oxygen*.
Lucy.index: the horse: *Equus*, the kind alive today, by about 4 million years ago (the Hagerman horses of Idaho, about 4 to 3 million years old). The elephant line: mammoths reach Europe and Asia, about 3 million years ago.
Lucy.picturesWanted: Lucy's skeleton laid out (the cast; National Museum of Ethiopia or Cleveland Museum of Natural History; licence to ask); the Laetoli footprints (Commons; licence to check).
Lucy.summary: A warm world, warmer than now, with the sea higher. In East Africa, apes that walked upright lived by rivers and lakes. Lucy is the best known of them. At the end, ice began to grow in the north.

more.spanLine: From about 5.3 to 2.6 million years ago.
paragraphs: About 3.2 million years ago, at Hadar, in what is now the Afar Region of Ethiopia, a river wound across a wide, flat plain and sometimes flooded it, and a lake to the east rose and fell. Lucy lived there. She was a little over a metre tall and walked upright on two legs, though her arms were long and strong. Her bones are now in the National Museum of Ethiopia, in Addis Ababa, and in Ethiopia she is also called Dinkinesh, Amharic for "you are marvellous" (*Lucy*).

Lucy's kind lived from about 3.9 to 2.9 million years ago. So no one like Lucy has been found from the start of this stretch, or from its end. The stretch is named for who you would meet in the middle.

Others like her walked across East Africa. At Laetoli, in Tanzania, about 3.6 million years ago, three of them walked over damp volcanic ash. The ash set hard, and their trail of footprints, about seventy of them, is still there.

That is what is new: apes that walked upright on the ground, in many places. Others that may have walked upright lived even earlier (*Walking upright*). In this stretch there were several kinds of them. About 3.3 million years ago, beside what is now Lake Turkana, in Kenya, someone struck flakes off stones (*Stone tools*).
The whole Earth was perhaps two or three degrees warmer than today, and the sea stood perhaps fifteen or twenty metres higher. North and South America came together at Panama (*Panama closes*).
Two million seven hundred thousand years is half the Ice line. That is a little longer than all the time from its end until now.

Geologists call this stretch the Pliocene ("PLY-o-seen"), Greek for "more recent". Charles Lyell published the name in 1833. Until 2009 it ran to 1.8 million years ago. Then geologists moved its end to 2.58 million years ago, where the ice begins.
At its end, ice sheets began to grow over the north of the world, and to melt, and to grow again (*Ice by turns*).

Hand axes.name: Hand axes
Hand axes.spanNote: the start a dated boundary at a point in the rock: 2.58 (Monte San Nicola, near Gela, Sicily); the end not an official boundary: 1 million years is the middle of the slow change from ice ages of about 41,000 years to ice ages of about 100,000 (about 1.25 to 0.7 million years ago), kept by Michael (10 Oct). The nearest official edges are 1.80 and 0.774.
Hand axes.officialName: the first two parts of the Pleistocene, "most recent": the Gelasian, after Gela in Sicily, and most of the Calabrian, after Calabria
Hand axes.knownFrom: stone tools and bones in the rift valleys of East Africa and at Dmanisi, in Georgia, and shells in seafloor mud, which record the ice
Hand axes.insideIt: events *Ice by turns* (at the start edge). Plots: *Sea level*, *Oxygen*.

Hand axes.summary: Ice sheets grew in the north and melted again, about every forty thousand years. In East Africa, people of a new kind made the oldest hand axes found, and others of their family walked as far as Georgia.

more.spanLine: From about 2.6 million to 1 million years ago.
paragraphs: At Kokiselei, near the west shore of Lake Turkana, in Kenya, there are stones that someone shaped about 1.76 million years ago. Each was struck again and again on both sides, until it had a point and two long cutting edges, the shape of a big almond. These are among the oldest hand axes yet found. Beside them lie simpler tools, sharp flakes knocked off pebbles, the kind people in Africa had already been making for more than a million years.
That is what is new: a tool made to a plan, the same shape again and again. Hand axes like these were made for more than a million and a half years, across Africa, Europe and Asia.
Yet no hand axes have been found from the first eight hundred thousand years of this stretch. The name marks what you would find in it, not what was there at the start.

They were probably made by *Homo erectus* ("HO-mo ee-RECK-tus"), people about as tall as people today. Near Kokiselei, at Nariokotome, Kamoya Kimeu found in 1984 nearly the whole skeleton of a boy of that kind, about 1.5 million years old. About 1.8 million years ago, people of the same family lived at Dmanisi, in Georgia, far from Africa. They made only the simpler tools.

All through the stretch, ice sheets grew over the north of the world and melted away again, about every forty-one thousand years (*Ice by turns*). Mammoths in Europe were bigger than elephants are now.
One million six hundred thousand years is about a third of the Ice line.

Geologists call this stretch the first part of the Pleistocene ("PLY-sto-seen"), Greek for "most recent", a name Charles Lyell made in 1839. They split it into the Gelasian ("jel-AY-zhun"), after the town of Gela, in Sicily, and the Calabrian, after Calabria, in the south of Italy. Neither ends at a million years. That edge is ours, set in the middle of a slow change in the ice.
Near the end of the stretch, the cold spells began to last longer, about a hundred thousand years each.

Yonas Beyene and others, "The characteristics and chronology of the earliest Acheulean at Konso, Ethiopia," *PNAS*, 2013. Hand axes nearly as old, in Ethiopia.
Frank Brown, John Harris, Richard Leakey and Alan Walker, "Early *Homo erectus* skeleton from west Lake Turkana, Kenya," *Nature*, 1985. The Nariokotome boy.
Ian Tattersall, *Masters of the Planet* (Palgrave Macmillan, 2012). For a parent.

Mammoths.spanNote: the start not an official boundary (see *Hand axes*)

Mammoths.knownFrom: ice cores, back more than 800,000 years; shells in seafloor mud; and bones, teeth and genes in frozen ground

Mammoths.index: the elephant line: the woolly mammoth, about 3 metres at the shoulder and about 6 tonnes, from about 800,000 years ago, and the bigger steppe mammoth before it. The horse: *Equus*, across the cold north.

Mammoths.summary: The ice ages grew longer. Each round of cold and warm took about a hundred thousand years, most of it cold. Across the cold north, on dry grassland that ran from Spain to Alaska, lived mammoths.

more.spanLine: From about 1 million years ago to now.
paragraphs: In the frozen ground of north-eastern Siberia, in Sakha, mammoth teeth have lain for more than a million years. In 2021 a team led by Tom van der Valk and Love Dalén read genes from three of them. Two of the teeth are more than a million years old, and their genes were older than any read before them. The third, younger, came from one of the earliest woolly mammoths.

A big male woolly mammoth stood about three metres at the shoulder and weighed about six tonnes, as much as a big African elephant. It had long hair, small ears and a short tail. The steppe mammoth before it was bigger still.

That is what is new: long ice ages. Each round of cold and warm lasted about a hundred thousand years, most of it cold. The warm spells lasted about ten to thirty thousand. In the cold spells a dry grassland ran across the north, from Spain to Alaska, and mammoths, woolly rhinos, horses and bison grazed it.
Ice from this stretch still exists. In Antarctica, one core of ice holds the last 800,000 years without a break, and the bubbles in it hold the air of each cold spell and each warm one.
About 774,000 years ago, the Earth's magnetic field flipped. Before then, a compass would have pointed south instead of north. It has not flipped since.
People of our own species lived in Africa by about 315,000 years ago (*Homo sapiens*), and made beads of shells by about 142,000 (*Shell beads*).
A million years is a fifth of the Ice line.

Geologists split this stretch four ways. One part is the Chibanian ("chee-BAH-nee-un"), after Chiba, in Japan, where the rock records the last flip of the magnetic field. It is the first name on the geologists' chart taken from a place in Japan.
The last mammoths lived on Wrangel Island, in the Arctic Ocean, until about 4,000 years ago, when the pyramids of Egypt were already old.

references: Tom van der Valk and others, "Million-year-old DNA sheds light on the genomic history of mammoths," *Nature*, 2021. The scene.
Jean Jouzel and others, "Orbital and millennial Antarctic climate variability over the past 800,000 years," *Science*, 2007. The ice of this stretch.
Marianne Dehasque and others, "Temporal dynamics of woolly mammoth genome erosion prior to extinction," *Cell*, 2024. Wrangel Island.
Adrian Lister and Paul Bahn, *Mammoths: Giants of the Ice Age* (University of California Press, revised edition 2007). For a parent.

The last ice age.spanNote: the start is our rounding of 129,000, the base of the Upper Pleistocene on the chart, which is provisional (ratified as a name in 2020, with no point in the rock yet); the warm spell itself began a little before

The last ice age.summary: One whole swing of the ice: a warm spell about as warm as now, a long cold one, and the warm one that has lasted since. Everything on the Time Machine happens in about its last twelve thousand years.

more.spanLine: From about 130,000 years ago to now.
paragraphs: In the north-west of Greenland, at a camp called NEEM, a team from fourteen countries drilled down through the ice sheet. In July 2010 the drill reached the rock below, about two and a half kilometres down. Near the bottom the ice was folded, like a rug pushed against a wall, and the team had to put its layers back in order. They did it by matching the air trapped in its bubbles with the air in ice cores from elsewhere. The oldest snow they could put in order fell about 128,000 years ago, at the start of this stretch.

That old ice says it was warm. In north Greenland the air was about eight degrees warmer than in the last thousand years, and in summer the top of the ice sheet melted. Yet the ice sheet thinned by only about four hundred metres.

That is what is new: one whole swing of the ice, from warm to cold to warm. After the warm spell (*Hippos in London*), the cold came back slowly, over about a hundred thousand years, and ice sheets spread across the north (*Ice sheets*). At the coldest, about 20,000 years ago, the sea stood about 130 metres below today's (*Last glacial maximum*). Then, about 11,700 years ago, the cold broke in a few decades (*Ice lets go*).

Of all the swings, this is the one known best. Greenland's ice, read in order, reaches back only to about the start of this stretch, and radiocarbon can date a bone or a piece of charcoal only up to about fifty thousand years old. Most of the paintings, carvings and flutes on the deep line are in this stretch.
A hundred and thirty thousand years is about an eighth of the Mammoths line.
Geologists call the first part of it the Late Pleistocene and the last 11,700 years the Holocene. They have not yet chosen the point in the rock where the Late Pleistocene begins.
Everything on the Time Machine, from the end of the ice to now, fits in less than a tenth of this stretch.

Richard Alley, *The Two-Mile Time Machine* (Princeton University Press, 2000). For a parent.
