Hippos in London.name: Hippos in London
Hippos in London.spanNote: both edges rounded guesses, not official boundaries: the warm spell began about 130,000 years ago by the ocean's shells (about 126,000 by Europe's pollen), and the sea began to fall from its high about 116,000 years ago
Hippos in London.officialName: none of its own; climate scientists call it the Last Interglacial, or the Eemian, after the river Eem in the Netherlands; in Britain, the Ipswichian
Hippos in London.knownFrom: bones, pollen and beetles in old river gravel, beaches and corals above today's sea, and the bottom of the Greenland ice
Hippos in London.insideIt: no events yet. Plots: *Sea level* (the high), *Oxygen*, *People*.
Hippos in London.index: the elephant line: the straight-tusked elephant, not a mammoth, under Trafalgar Square.
Hippos in London.picturesWanted: the hippo bones from Trafalgar Square (Natural History Museum, London; licence to ask); the Barrington hippo (Sedgwick Museum, Cambridge; licence to ask).
Hippos in London.summary: A warm spell, about as warm as now. Hippos lived in the Thames, lions where Trafalgar Square is now, and the sea stood several metres higher. In Britain there were no people at all.

more.spanLine: From about 130,000 to 115,000 years ago.
paragraphs: Trafalgar Square, in the middle of London, stands on gravel that the Thames laid down long ago. In the 1950s, builders digging on the south side of the square found bones in the gravel. There were bones of hippopotamus, lion and rhinoceros, and of an elephant with straight tusks, bigger than any elephant alive today. The Natural History Museum keeps a hippo's tooth from under the square. It is about 125,000 years old.
Hippos lived all over England and Wales then. Their bones have been found in more than thirty-five places, as far north as the River Tees.

That is what is new: warmth. It was the last time the world was about as warm as it is now. Summers in southern England were up to about four degrees warmer than now, and the winters about the same. Ice at the poles shrank, and the sea stood six to nine metres higher than today's.

There were no people in Britain at all. Britain was an island, and the Neanderthals living in Europe did not cross to it before the sea rose. People did not come back until about sixty thousand years ago.
No hippo has lived wild in Britain since.
Fifteen thousand years is about a ninth of the last ice age. It is longer than everything on the Time Machine.

The stretch has no official name of its own. Climate scientists call it the Last Interglacial, which means the last warm spell between two cold ones, or the Eemian ("EE-mee-un"), after the river Eem in the Netherlands, where its sea shells were first described. In Britain it is called the Ipswichian.
About 116,000 years ago, the sea began to fall.

Andrea Dutton and others, "Sea-level rise due to polar ice-sheet mass loss during past warm periods," *Science*, 2015. How high the sea stood.
G. Russell Coope, "The climatic significance of coleopteran assemblages from the Eemian deposits in southern England," *Netherlands Journal of Geosciences*, 2000. How warm, from beetles.

Ice sheets.name: Ice sheets
Ice sheets.spanNote: the start a rounded guess, when the sea began to fall (about 116,000); the end a dated boundary at a point in the ice: 11,700 years before 2000, at 1,492.45 metres in the NGRIP2 core, Greenland
Ice sheets.officialName: none for the cold spell alone; it is most of the Late Pleistocene, and is called the last glacial: the Devensian in Britain, the Weichselian in northern Europe, the Wisconsin in North America
Ice sheets.knownFrom: ice cores, the rubble and scratched rock the ice sheets left, the floors of shallow seas, and radiocarbon dates on bones, charcoal and wood
Ice sheets.insideIt: events *Blombos Cave*, *Sulawesi*, *Lebombo bone*, *Flutes*, *El Castillo*, *Hohle Fels Venus*, *Chauvet*, *Lady of Brassempouy*, *Lascaux*, *Ishango bone*, *Altamira*, *Last glacial maximum*, *Ice lets go* (at the end edge). Plots: *Sea level*, *Oxygen*, *People*.
Ice sheets.index: the woolly mammoth, on the dry grassland of the north and on the floor of the North Sea.
Ice sheets.picturesWanted: a mammoth tooth hauled up by a fishing boat (Natural History Museum, Rotterdam, or Urk's museum; licence to ask); the Colinda point (British Museum; licence to check).
Ice sheets.summary: The cold came back. Ice sheets kilometres thick spread over Canada and northern Europe, and the sea fell so far that the southern North Sea and the Bering Strait were dry land.

more.spanLine: From about 115,000 to 11,700 years ago.
paragraphs: Every so often a fishing boat in the North Sea hauls up something strange in its net: a mammoth's tooth, the bone of a wild ox, a piece of antler shaped by a person. Fishermen from the Dutch town of Urk have long sold the mammoth teeth they bring up. The bones come from the floor of the sea. When the sea was low, that floor was dry land, and people now call it Doggerland.
In 1931 the *Colinda*, a fishing boat from Lowestoft, hauled up a lump of peat off the coast of Norfolk. Inside it was a spear point of antler, with barbs, about 13,500 years old.

That is what is new: ice sheets, ice so thick it buried mountains. Over Hudson Bay, in Canada, it was about three kilometres thick, perhaps more. Chicago lay under about half a mile of it (*Last glacial maximum*). So much water was locked up in ice that, at the coldest, about 20,000 years ago, the sea stood about 130 metres below today's. The southern North Sea was a plain of rivers, hills and marshes, joining Britain to the rest of Europe. The northern part lay under ice. Asia and America were joined by a broad plain more than a thousand kilometres across, where the Bering Strait is now.
The cold was not steady. In Greenland the ice records more than twenty sudden warmings, some of more than ten degrees in a few decades, each followed by a slower return of the cold.

People of our own species lived through it on every continent but Antarctica. In this stretch they made the oldest paintings and flutes yet found (*Sulawesi*, *Flutes*), and drew and carved (*Blombos Cave*).
A hundred and three thousand years is four fifths of the last ice age.
The stretch has no official name of its own. In Britain it is called the Devensian, in northern Europe the Weichselian, and in North America the Wisconsin.
About 11,700 years ago, in a few decades, the cold broke (*Ice lets go*).

Hans Peeters and Garry Momber, "The southern North Sea and the human occupation of northwest Europe after the Last Glacial Maximum," *Netherlands Journal of Geosciences*, 2014. Doggerland and the Colinda point.
Willi Dansgaard and others, "Evidence for general instability of past climate from a 250-kyr ice-core record," *Nature*, 1993. The sudden warmings.
Vincent Gaffney, Simon Fitch and David Smith, *Europe's Lost World: The Rediscovery of Doggerland* (Council for British Archaeology, 2009). For a parent.

Since 2018 it has three parts: the Greenlandian, the Northgrippian (from 8,200 years ago) and the Meghalayan (from 4,200, after Meghalaya, in India).

After the ice.summary: The great ice sheets melted and did not come back. The sea rose, the Sahara was green and then dried, and people began to farm. Nearly everything on the Time Machine happens here.

more.spanLine: From about 11,700 years ago to now.
paragraphs: At Gobero, in Niger, on the edge of the Ténéré desert, the sand holds about two hundred graves, and the bones of the fish the people there caught. When people lived there, Gobero was the shore of a lake. Nile perch nearly two metres long swam in it, with crocodiles and hippos. The people fished with harpoons and hooks of bone. They lived there twice: from about 9,650 to 8,150 years ago, and again from about 7,150 to 4,450 years ago.

For thousands of years the summer rains of Africa reached far north, and much of the Sahara was grassland, with lakes. One lake, Mega-Chad, was about the size of the Caspian Sea. On the rocks of Tassili n'Ajjer, in Algeria, people drew hippos and cattle (*Green Sahara*). Then, from about 5,500 years ago, the rains moved south again. How fast the Sahara dried is argued.

That is what is new: the warm that came after the ice, and stayed. The ice that covered the north melted, and it did not come back in the winter. The great ice sheets took thousands of years to melt, and the sea rose with them. By about 7,000 years ago it was within a few metres of where it is now. Doggerland drowned (*Storegga slide*), and Britain became an island. The last mammoths died on Wrangel Island, about 4,000 years ago.
In this stretch, people began to farm, in several places on their own. They built cities, and they wrote. All of it, farms, cities, writing, ships, is on the Time Machine.
Eleven thousand seven hundred years is less than a tenth of the last ice age, and about a hundredth of the Mammoths line.
Geologists call this stretch the Holocene ("HOL-o-seen"), Greek for "wholly recent". Its start is not marked in rock. It is marked in ice, at a depth of 1,492.45 metres in an ice core from Greenland.
On the Time Machine, the years are counted from about then.
